title: Strings and string manipulation
summary: Clean up messy text with string methods such as strip(), lower() and title(), and build sentences with f-strings.
objectives: Fix inconsistent capital letters with .lower() and .title()
Build a sentence from variables with an f-string

segments.title: What you will build
segments.body:
## What you will build

Text typed by people is messy: extra spaces at the ends, capital letters in odd places. In this lab you start with a raw name like `"   aLiCe joHNson   "` and clean it into `Alice Johnson` using the string methods `.strip()`, `.lower()` and `.title()`. Then you use the clean name inside an f-string to build a friendly greeting and print it. Cleaning input before you use it is something every real program has to do, from sign-up forms to chatbots.

lab.title: Clean up a name
lab.objective: Turn a messy raw string into a tidy name with string methods, then greet the person with an f-string.
lab.instructions:
The variable raw_name holds a messy name with extra spaces at both ends and letters in the wrong case. Do not change raw_name itself; make a cleaned copy.

1. Remove the spaces at both ends with .strip().
2. Make all the letters lowercase with .lower(), then give each word a capital first letter with .title(). You can chain the methods one after another on the same line.
3. Store the result in clean_name. For the given raw_name it should be Alice Johnson.
4. Build the greeting with an f-string and store it in greeting. It must read exactly:

Hello, Alice Johnson! Welcome to NeuroMind.

5. Print greeting.
lab.constraints: Keep the variable names raw_name, clean_name and greeting. Do not edit the text inside raw_name and do not type the clean name by hand; let the string methods produce it. Print only the greeting. Do not use input().
lab.starter_code:
raw_name = "   aLiCe joHNson   "

# 1. Remove the spaces at both ends with .strip()
# 2. Fix the case with .lower() and then .title()
# 3. Store the cleaned name in clean_name
clean_name = raw_name

# 4. Build the greeting with an f-string:
#    Hello, <clean name>! Welcome to NeuroMind.
greeting = ""

# 5. Print the greeting
print(greeting)
hints: String methods give back a new string; they do not change the old one. So you need clean_name = raw_name.something(), not raw_name.something() on its own.
You can chain methods: raw_name.strip().lower().title() does all three steps in one go. Store the result in clean_name.
An f-string starts with f and puts a variable inside curly braces: greeting = f"Hello, {clean_name}! Welcome to NeuroMind." and then print(greeting).

What you print is the greeting

raw_name is still messy and clean_name was made from it

tests.remediation: Use clean_name = raw_name.strip().lower().title(). Each method returns a new string, so store the result.

tests.label: greeting is the full greeting sentence
tests.remediation: Build it with an f-string: greeting = f"Hello, {clean_name}! Welcome to NeuroMind." Check the comma, the exclamation mark and the full stop.

definition.description: What you print is the greeting
definition.name: greeting

tests.label: The printed line is exactly the greeting sentence
tests.remediation: Your output must be exactly Hello, Alice Johnson! Welcome to NeuroMind. on one line, with no extra words or lines.

tests.label: raw_name is still messy and clean_name was made from it
tests.remediation: Leave raw_name exactly as given and do not type Alice Johnson yourself. Make clean_name from raw_name with .strip(), .lower() and .title().

lab.solution:
raw_name = "   aLiCe joHNson   "

clean_name = raw_name.strip().lower().title()

greeting = f"Hello, {clean_name}! Welcome to NeuroMind."

print(greeting)
